public_rationale: The claim is that, judged by robustness, generalization to new situations and autonomous goal-directed behavior, AI systems at the time still fell short. ARC-AGI-3 was released in March 2026. It drops agents into unfamiliar environments with no instructions and no stated goals. Frontier models scored under 1%, including Claude Opus 4.6, which was available when the post appeared. Humans solved all the environments. That is a large, measured gap on exactly the abilities the claim names. Some experts argued in Nature that human-level AI had already arrived, but that is an opinion piece, not a measurement. 'Remain limited' is a modest claim, and the evidence supports it.
limitations: The decisive benchmark results came out about five weeks after the post.
ARC-AGI-3 is one benchmark, and its scoring heavily penalizes inefficiency.
'Original AGI definitions' are paraphrased by the speaker.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: By original AGI standards, current AI systems remain limited.

statement.excerpt: By the standards articulated in the original definitions of artificial general intelligence—robustness across environments, reliable generalization under novelty, and autonomous goal-directed behavior—current AI systems remain limited.
statement.document_title: Rumors of AGI’s arrival have been greatly exaggerated

from_speaker: by the standards articulated in the original definitions of AGI
our_interpretation: Plain reading: in February 2026, frontier AI systems clearly fell short of human-level robustness, generalization to novel situations, and autonomous goal-directed behavior.

'Current AI systems' means the frontier systems available at the post date (for example Claude Opus 4.6, released February 2026). The target period runs from February 2026 through March 2026, so that it covers the first independent evaluations of those same systems. This choice is flagged as an ambiguity.

'Remain limited' is a weak claim. It is supported if public evaluations of those systems show a large gap from human performance on tests built for novel environments and self-directed goal discovery.
criteria.support_condition: Independent evaluations of frontier systems from the period show large shortfalls against humans on tasks requiring generalization to novel environments, inferring goals without instructions, or robust autonomous behavior.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Independent evaluations from the period show frontier systems matching humans on novel-environment, goal-discovery and robustness tests without task-specific help.

evidence.excerpt: Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro led the pack at 0.37%. OpenAI’s GPT-5.4 came in at 0.26%. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6 managed 0.25%, while xAI’s Grok-4.20 scored exactly zero. Humans, meanwhile, solved 100% of environments.
evidence.explanation: On a benchmark built to test generalization in novel environments, frontier systems from the period (including Claude Opus 4.6, released before the post) scored under 1%. Humans solved every environment. This is a large shortfall on the speaker's named standards.

evidence.excerpt: drop an AI agent into an unfamiliar game-like world with zero instructions, zero stated goals, and no description of the rules. The agent has to explore, figure out what it's supposed to do, form a plan, and execute it.
evidence.explanation: Shows the test targets the same abilities the claim names: generalization under novelty and autonomous goal-directed behavior.

evidence.excerpt: challenges AI agents to explore novel environments, acquire goals on the fly, build adaptable world models, and learn continuously.
